clinicalPearls: Caused by truncating variants in KAT6B, the same histone acetyltransferase implicated in genitopatellar syndrome, with variant position within the gene influencing which of the two allelic phenotypes emerges
Blepharophimosis with ptosis and a mask-like, relatively immobile face is characteristic and helps separate SBBYSS from genitopatellar syndrome
Marked infantile hypotonia, feeding difficulties and global developmental delay are consistent findings
Long thumbs and long great toes are a useful and distinctive skeletal clue
Dental anomalies, lacrimal duct obstruction, hypothyroidism and patellar abnormalities are frequently reported
Congenital heart defects and hearing loss may occur and should be actively sought
The disorder belongs to the KAT6B-related acetyltransferase group of chromatinopathies and is confirmed by molecular testing
reference.pathophysiology: KAT6B encodes a MYST-family lysine acetyltransferase that acetylates histone H3 to create chromatin states permissive for the transcription of developmental genes. In SBBYSS, truncating variants located in regions distinct from those causing genitopatellar syndrome disturb this acetylation-dependent regulation, disrupting developmental programmes governing the eyelids and face, muscle tone, the thyroid and the skeleton. The resulting epigenetic dysregulation produces the characteristic blepharophimosis and mask-like facies, hypotonia, long digits and endocrine and cardiac features, illustrating how the site of a variant in a single chromatin-modifier gene can shape strikingly different clinical pictures.
additionalDifferentials: Other forms of Ohdo syndrome (MASA/Maat-Kievit-Brunner, KAT6B-negative)
Congenital myasthenic and congenital myopathic disorders causing ptosis and hypotonia
Other syndromic intellectual disability with ptosis
additionalInvestigations: Exome or genome sequencing to identify KAT6B variants with attention to variant location
Thyroid function testing to detect hypothyroidism
Echocardiography to screen for congenital heart disease
Ophthalmological assessment for ptosis, blepharophimosis and lacrimal duct obstruction
Evaluation of feeding and swallowing in infancy
redFlags: Ptosis obscuring the visual axis and threatening amblyopia
Severe feeding difficulty with faltering growth in infancy
Untreated hypothyroidism that could worsen developmental outcome
reference.prognosis: The condition is generally compatible with survival into adulthood; intellectual disability is usual and ranges from mild to severe, and outcome is improved by early treatment of correctable problems such as hypothyroidism, ptosis and feeding difficulty alongside sustained developmental support.
pitfalls: Conflating SBBYSS with genitopatellar syndrome, which differ in prognosis and management despite sharing a gene
Missing hypothyroidism, which is treatable and affects development
Overlooking ptosis severe enough to cause amblyopia
Attributing the ptosis and hypotonia to a primary neuromuscular disorder without genetic testing
references: GeneReviews — KAT6B-Related Disorders (Genitopatellar Syndrome and SBBYSS)
Nature Reviews — histone acetyltransferases in development and disease
management: Correct hypothyroidism with levothyroxine replacement when detected on screening
Provide feeding support in infancy, including nasogastric or gastrostomy feeding for significant hypotonia-related difficulty
Refer for surgical correction of ptosis and blepharophimosis and for management of lacrimal duct obstruction
Manage congenital heart defects with cardiology input and surgical repair as indicated
Address hearing loss with audiological assessment and hearing aids or other support
Deliver early developmental intervention with physiotherapy, occupational, and speech therapy for hypotonia and developmental delay
Coordinate multidisciplinary care and offer genetic counselling, noting most KAT6B variants arise de novo
